external_sources.title: Earlier-class prior-learning crosswalk: SS1/SS2 Agriculture for SS3 First Term
external_sources.content: Prior-learning crosswalk for SS3 Agricultural Science First-Term revision. The owner-supplied SS1 archive SHA-256 is 024487129a86c3a89e55293b3ad71b0dfe8b8969ea55bbc64dbfdc17565c9a3e. Its SS1 First-Term Agricultural Science member SHA-256 is df1b516cdd8855d069a329d7aa627dbd0dcd3612dd10d254c53af9cb93a56526; the SS1 Third-Term member SHA-256 is 9e920bff3769d9d977c4b2849cc77c769b6033be9176f4f6b35c27935999e12a. SS1 First-Term Week 1 covers agricultural extension and education, animal health, finance and marketing; Week 3 covers marketing systems; Week 4 identifies agricultural loan/credit schemes and the National Agricultural Insurance Scheme; Week 5 covers crop and animal improvement; Week 7 introduces fishery, fish farming and fish ponds. SS1 Third-Term Weeks 6 and 9-10 cover artificial insemination and livestock management, including animal health, diseases and parasites. SS2 Third-Term Agricultural Science member SHA-256 6abb32818845fa3739f287d2cc3e274149313bfb381074a623a2bce8c02b2811 covers Animal Nutrition in Weeks 9-10. This is a cross-class evidence summary, not a new SS3 instructional lesson. It establishes topic presence in earlier-class curriculum but does not certify instructional depth or specialist approval.

units.subject: Agricultural Science
units.title: Exam Revision: Animal Nutrition and Malnutrition
objectives: Review the key terms and processes for Animal Nutrition and Malnutrition.
Apply the topic to WAEC, NECO and JAMB command words and structured responses.
units.body:
EXAM-PREPARATION REVISION BRIEF

Animal nutrition covers the energy, protein, minerals, vitamins, water and fibre needed for maintenance, growth, reproduction and production. A balanced ration matches the species and production stage. Malnutrition includes undernutrition, nutrient deficiency and harmful excess or imbalance. Causes include inadequate feed, poor feed quality, parasites, disease, competition and poor management. In exam answers, distinguish starvation from a specific nutrient deficiency and link signs to the likely nutritional problem.

WAEC / NECO / JAMB response approach: define the key term, organise the answer under the command word, give accurate examples and explain cause-and-effect relationships. For a comparison, state both sides using the same basis. For a process, write the stages in sequence. For a calculation, show the formula, substitution, units and final interpretation. These are revision notes and original exam-style practice; they are not a new SS3 instructional lesson and are not copied past questions.

objectives: Review the key terms and processes for Agricultural Extension.

units.body:
EXAM-PREPARATION REVISION BRIEF

Agricultural extension connects research, practical knowledge and farmers so they can make informed production decisions. Objectives include improving productivity, income, food security and resource management. Methods include individual contact such as farm visits, group methods such as demonstrations and field days, and mass communication such as radio and digital channels. Extension is two-way: agents listen, explain options, adapt advice to local conditions and gather feedback. Adoption is affected by cost, risk, literacy, trust, culture and input availability.

WAEC / NECO / JAMB response approach: define the key term, organise the answer under the command word, give accurate examples and explain cause-and-effect relationships. For a comparison, state both sides using the same basis. For a process, write the stages in sequence. For a calculation, show the formula, substitution, units and final interpretation. These are revision notes and original exam-style practice; they are not a new SS3 instructional lesson and are not copied past questions.

practice.question: State seven objectives of agricultural extension.
practice.answer_locator: Authored model answer; not represented as a source-printed answer key.
practice.answer: The source lists six objectives: educate farmers to replace less productive traditional methods with improved scientific techniques; improve rural living standards; identify proper marketing channels; help farmers access and supervise agricultural loans; link farmers with research institutes; and accelerate rural development. The source asks for seven but lists only six; a seventh is not invented.
practice.explanation: The source-body count does not reconcile with its seven-point question. This authored answer lists only the six objectives actually present and leaves the seventh unresolved for subject review.

objectives: Review the key terms and processes for Fish Farming.

units.body:
EXAM-PREPARATION REVISION BRIEF

Fish farming is the controlled rearing of fish for food or sale. Site selection considers clean water, soil that holds water, suitable topography, access, market proximity, security and flood risk. Production systems include ponds, tanks and cages. Good management includes pond preparation, suitable fingerlings, appropriate stocking density, balanced feed, water-quality monitoring, disease prevention and timely harvesting. Fish require suitable dissolved oxygen, temperature and pH. Overfeeding and excessive stocking can worsen water quality and increase disease risk.

units.body:
EXAM-PREPARATION REVISION BRIEF

Artificial insemination places semen into the female reproductive tract by a trained operator without natural mating. A programme includes selecting healthy breeding males, collecting semen hygienically, evaluating semen quality, diluting and preserving it, detecting oestrus and inseminating at the appropriate time. Benefits include wider use of selected sires and improved breeding records. Limitations include training and equipment costs, the need for accurate heat detection and careful semen handling. Poor hygiene or timing reduces success and can spread disease.

EXAM-PREPARATION REVISION BRIEF

Agricultural finance provides and manages money for farm establishment, production, processing and marketing. Fixed capital purchases long-term assets such as buildings and machinery; working capital pays recurring costs such as seed, feed, labour and transport. Sources include savings, cooperatives, banks, microfinance institutions, government programmes and value-chain partners. A loan should match the farm cash-flow cycle and repayment capacity. A farm budget estimates costs and returns; cash-flow records show when money enters and leaves. Borrowers should understand interest, collateral, fees and repayment terms.

units.body:
EXAM-PREPARATION REVISION BRIEF

Agricultural insurance transfers specified financial risks from a farmer to an insurer in return for a premium, subject to policy terms. A policy states the insured subject, covered event, exclusions, sum insured, premium, deductible and claim procedure. Insurance does not prevent hazards; it can reduce financial shock after a covered loss. Farmers should disclose material facts, keep production and purchase records, follow risk-reduction requirements and report losses promptly. A claim is assessed against the policy and evidence; not every loss is automatically payable.

EXAM-PREPARATION REVISION BRIEF

Agricultural marketing moves farm products from producers to consumers. Activities include assembling, grading, sorting, packaging, storage, transport, processing, wholesaling, retailing and market information. A marketing channel describes the route a product follows, such as farmer to cooperative to wholesaler to retailer to consumer. Price is affected by quality, season, supply, demand, transport, storage and bargaining power. Post-harvest losses reduce saleable quantity and income. Market information helps farmers decide what to produce, when to sell and where to sell.

units.body:
EXAM-PREPARATION REVISION BRIEF

Routine animal-management practices maintain health, welfare and productivity. They include suitable feed and clean water, species-appropriate housing and ventilation, cleaning pens and equipment, safe manure removal, daily observation, isolation of sick or newly arrived animals, records and veterinary care. Other practices may include identification, vaccination and parasite control under competent guidance. Handling should minimise fear, pain and injury. Biosecurity reduces the introduction and spread of pathogens through people, animals, equipment, feed and water.

units.title: Exam Revision: Principles of Animal Health Management
objectives: Review the key terms and processes for Principles of Animal Health Management.
Apply the topic to WAEC, NECO and JAMB command words and structured responses.
units.body:
EXAM-PREPARATION REVISION BRIEF

Animal health management prevents disease, detects problems early and protects animal welfare and public health. Disease risk is influenced by the host, the infectious agent and the environment. Prevention includes clean housing, nutrition, safe water, ventilation, reduced stress, quarantine, vaccination where recommended, parasite management and veterinary assessment. Biosecurity controls movement of animals, people, equipment and materials that may carry pathogens. Surveillance and records help identify unusual illness or production changes. Responsible antimicrobial use helps limit antimicrobial resistance.

WAEC / NECO / JAMB response approach: define the key term, organise the answer under the command word, give accurate examples and explain cause-and-effect relationships. For a comparison, state both sides using the same basis. For a process, write the stages in sequence. For a calculation, show the formula, substitution, units and final interpretation. These are revision notes and original exam-style practice; they are not a new SS3 instructional lesson and are not copied past questions.

units.body:
EXAM-PREPARATION REVISION BRIEF

Animal-disease exam questions require learners to connect a disease with its cause, signs, transmission, effects and control. Signs may include fever, diarrhoea, coughing, lameness, skin lesions, reduced appetite or production decline; they are not always specific to one disease. Transmission may occur through direct contact, aerosols, contaminated feed or water, vectors, equipment or animal products. Control depends on the disease and may include isolation, hygiene, vaccination, vector control, movement restrictions, safe carcass disposal and veterinary diagnosis. Zoonotic diseases also require attention to human exposure and food safety.

WAEC / NECO / JAMB response approach: define the key term, organise the answer under the command word, give accurate examples and explain cause-and-effect relationships. For a comparison, state both sides using the same basis. For a process, write the stages in sequence. For a calculation, show the formula, substitution, units and final interpretation. objectives: Review the key terms and processes for Livestock Parasites.
Apply the topic to WAEC, NECO and JAMB command words and structured responses.
units.body:
EXAM-PREPARATION REVISION BRIEF

Livestock parasites live on or in a host and obtain resources at the host's expense. Ectoparasites live on the body surface and include ticks, lice and mites. Endoparasites live inside the body and include gastrointestinal worms, flukes and some protozoa. Effects include irritation, blood loss, tissue damage, poor growth, reduced production, anaemia and transmission of pathogens. Control depends on the parasite and may include clean housing, pasture management, quarantine, observation and targeted treatment under veterinary guidance. Indiscriminate drug use can promote resistance.

WAEC / NECO / JAMB response approach: define the key term, organise the answer under the command word, give accurate examples and explain cause-and-effect relationships. For a comparison, state both sides using the same basis. For a process, write the stages in sequence. For a calculation, show the formula, substitution, units and final interpretation. These are revision notes and original exam-style practice; they are not a new SS3 instructional lesson and are not copied past questions.
